body:
I don't understand. Your rephrasing would prohibit h2 after h4, since 4 is not 1 less than, equal to, or greater than 2. The existing wording works: 4 is less than 2.

Similarly, both phrasings correctly ensure that only h2 (or h1) follows after h1. 2 is one greater than 1.

I'll close this, but happy to continue discussing and reopen if something was missed.

@domenic Sorry, that was a misunderstanding on my part. However, the misunderstanding resulted from the fact that "greater" and "less" may not be clear in the context of headings. If you compare e.g. h1 and h3, then
* h1 is greater than h3, both in terms of font size and in the programmatic hierarchy of headings.
* h1 is less than h3 only in terms of the number after the h.

I.e. the smaller the number the larger the hierarchical level of the heading.

If only I had this misunderstanding due to my lack of English knowledge, then it is only my mistake. If the misunderstanding can be of general nature, an additional example sentence would be perhaps meaningful, like "After a h3 may follow a h1, h2, h3 and h4, but no h5 or h6".

Well, note that it's not comparing the headings; it's comparing the heading levels. And the heading levels are pretty clearly defined as numbers. Numbers have known semantics for "greater" and "less".

There's already an example following that section, but more examples don't hurt! Please feel free to send a pull request.
@domenic [Native speakers have the same misunderstanding](https://github.com/w3c/wcag/discussions/2722) as I had, so an explanation would be useful
As I said, please feel free to send such a pull request!

@JAWS-test your OP assertion is not correct.  <q>a heading level that is less than</q> is correct.  <q>a heading level that is **_1_** less than</q> is not correct.

> after a h1 only a h2 should follow (1 less). 

That is not, and never has been AFAIK, part of any HTML specification.

> An h4 may be followed by an h2 (2 greater).

Yes, because the h2 is relative to a previous portion of the outline hierarchy.  If a heading following an h4 is to be a sibling of the parent to this h4, it would necessarily be h3.  This is why this section mentions heading **_lead_** and not just parent heading or previous heading.

It seems to me that <q>heading lead</q> is not a defined term, and I can understand how someone might read this line to mean essentially the opposite of what is meant.

> Each [heading](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html#concept-heading) following another [heading](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html#concept-heading) lead in the [outline](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html#outline) must have a [heading level](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html#heading-level) that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than lead's [heading level](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html#heading-level).

h1 is less than h3. so after an h3 you can have an h1. cool
but going the other way, "1 greater than" means that after an h3 you *must* have an h4 if you're going deeper (h4 is 1 greater than h3)

in essence, this seems to disallow skipping heading levels when going deeper down the hierarchy. which, i would argue, is a bit too restrictive. there are valid reasons (often technical) why an author may need to have, say, an h2 followed by and h4 rather than an h3 - all the scenarios like "they're embedding a piece of content from somewhere, and it's not known a priori what level it will be at" that originally were meant to be solved by the mythical outline algorithm.

or, to be clearer @domenic am i reading it right that based on the spec wording, the following is NOT valid because "h4 is not 1 greater than h1"? ``` html

Blah

...

Foo

...

```

> There's already an example following that section, but more examples don't hurt! Please feel free to send a pull request.

I cannot find the file to edit for a PR.  I think I can rewrite without using <q>heading lead</q> and <q>lead's heading level</q>.  I am browsing here:  https://github.com/whatwg/html

> am i reading it right that based on the spec wording, the following is NOT valid

Correct.

> because "h4 is not 1 greater than h1"?

Well, because 4 is not 1 greater than 1. Again, we're not talking about headings or tag names, which are elements or strings; we're talking about heading levels, which are numbers.

> I think I can rewrite without using "heading lead" and "lead's heading level".

Please don't do that. Declaring the _lead_ variable, with its clear type of "heading" is very helpful for clarity here. If you aren't able to decipher the algorithmic style here, please add an example, don't modify the already-very-clear algorithm (which goes from the _lead_ heading to _lead_'s heading level, which is a number).

> I cannot find the file to edit for a PR.

You can learn more about how to contribute to the HTML Standard here, including instructions for installing the build tools etc.: https://github.com/whatwg/meta/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

thanks for confirming, @domenic ... it does indeed look like some folks are getting confused by the fact that, in general parlance (at least in WCAG circles), "higher"/"lower" refers to the semantic/structural meaning (where a heading level 1 would be the "highest", hierarchically, and heading level 2, 3, etc are then respectively "lower")...whereas comparators in the HTML spec (higher, lower, greater than, less than) are all just looking at the raw number of the heading level.

Yeah, I don't really know how to make that clearer except maybe with an added example. Like... the definitions are right there, as hyperlinks.

> **heading level**, which is given by the number

> must have a [heading level](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html#heading-level) that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than

i grokked it, but perhaps a few more examples (like the one I used above, with the h4 following the h1) may help, don't know. one thing that did also confuse some folks was the term "heading *lead*", as this seems to be a fairly "programmery" term.

I will be honest though, I'm not particularly a fan of disallowing jumps of more than 1 when going into deeper hierarchies / greater heading levels - again for exactly the same situations (like the above, with the included bit of markup that doesn't know a priori what level it will be included at) that the original mythical outline algorithm. but i'll file that as a separate issue for discussion

@patrickhlauke and @bruce-usab From an accessibility perspective, not skipping headings makes sense, so we of all people should not oppose it. We also shouldn't pretend to be surprised about the requirement, because in the Accessibility rules for PDF this is a strict rule: https://www.powermapper.com/products/sortsite/rules/accmatterhorn/#checkpoint-14-headings.

Currently the rule is not checked by the W3C validator, but I have suggested to change this: https://github.com/validator/validator/issues/1441

>> I think I can rewrite without using "heading lead" and "lead's heading level".

> Please don't do that. Declaring the _lead_ variable, with its clear type of "heading" is very helpful for clarity here.

Okay, I think I am making sense of this.   In the excerpt "_lead's_ heading level" — _lead_ probably is not an `H` element.  Also, in "heading _lead_" the _lead_ might not be an `H` element, but I think "heading _lead_ must be an an `H` element.

Is _lead_ a defined term?

> If you aren't able to decipher the algorithmic style here, please add an example...

> I don't really know how to make that clearer except maybe with an added example.

As someone largely responsible for not being able to [define ICT](https://www.access-board.gov/ict/#E103.4) with resorting to examples, I feel your pain.

> ....don't modify the already-very-clear algorithm (which goes from the _lead_ heading to _lead_'s heading level, which is a number).

I is not so very clear because the section uses similar-but-not-identical words to mean the same thing, namely "lower" and "less than".  It is confusable.  For example, H1 is a lower level than H2.  But conceptually, H2 < H1.

> You can learn more about how to contribute to the HTML Standard here, including instructions for installing the build tools etc.: https://github.com/whatwg/meta/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

Thank you.

> Is _lead_ a defined term?

_lead_ is a variable. It is a heading (i.e. a hN element), because we used the phrasing "heading _lead_". This is like saying "number _x_" or "window _w_".

> But conceptually, H2 < H1.

I just disagree with this, and don't see any support for it in the spec.

The spec also always uses the words "lower" and "less than" when referring to heading levels, which are numbers.

Right, the spec is not aligned with how lay people talk about things using plain human language.

H2 is subordinate to H1.  H2 is under H1.  H2 is lower in the hierarchy than H1.  H2 is less than H1.

I submit that I am exactly at the limit of the technical audience that you wish to communicate with.  From that perspective, this portion of the spec lacks clarity.  My good faith reading has it saying the opposite of what it means to convey.

Yes, a counter-example of H4 following H2 and being declared to be invalid would be clarifying.  It would also be extremely helpful for the validator to throw an error (not a warning) when H4 follows H2 absent an H3.

I agree that the wording of this sentence is nonsensical, but not because of numeric levels, but because the way the word lead is used. From previous comments I can read out that the word lead is meant as a variable, which makes entire thing even more confusing.

"Each heading following another heading lead in the outline must have a heading level that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than lead's heading level."

"Each heading following another heading" - okay, an heading following another heading, perfectly makes sense. "lead in the outline" - what does lead mean in this context? - don't know, let's ignore this bit for now. "must have a heading level that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than lead's heading level." - What does lead mean here? "lead's heading level" implies to me that what's meant is the previous heading's heading level (leading heading aka heading ahead/before of current one). okay, so heading following another heading in the outline (tree structure) must be less than by any amount, equal or greater than by one. An h1 can then be followed by h1, h2. An h2 can be followed by h1, h2, h3.

Now we're back to wondering what does the first "lead" mean though? Entire sentence being "Each heading following another heading in the outline must have a heading level that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than lead's heading level." or "Each heading following another heading in the outline must have a heading level that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than previous heading's level.". Word "lead" can also mean the very first heading, which would always be h1.

Last interpretation I can come up with is "Each heading following another heading X in the outline must have a heading level that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than X's heading level.". Where X is an heading element. In which case the phrase "lead" is very terrible choice here as substitution to a variable such as X. Especially when there's no explanation following what variable "lead" is and when entire sentence can be simplified and phrased much simpler in basic English phrasing. Use of variables in explanations is usually for explaining a bit of code or a mathematical function.

Though this means structure like this is valid:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/36480939/205954632-a9d65393-976f-4a18-86b9-d44ad968dfaa.png)
I suggest everyone who is confused by the variable name _lead_ replace it with _x_, indeed. Hopefully that makes it easier to understand.

Issue is that without searching for answers from the Internet, I would have **never** assumed the word _lead_ is meant as a variable. It simply doesn't make sense. Documentations should be written as simply as possible with goal of zero ambiguity. Sadly HTML documentation fails that miserably at multiple spots - but hey, at least it is a good source for internet arguments.
